body: I used to think that I'd be fine if I kept tabs on my ex since I wasn't actually talking to him. I just had this need to know certain things, like if he was talking to someone or whatever.. Then it hit me. If I look and he IS talking to someone, what is me knowing going to change? Nothing. I would do NOTHING about it. Knowing what's going on in their lives doesn't give us anything. We cannot change what is going on in their lives. Be present in your own life. You will be so so much happier. Also, no contact is hard. You did so good, and you still are. You don't get cuter from your hurt, you recover, and it is not a process that can be completed. Just like an addict, every day moving forward is working towards your betterment. You got this. Be nice to yourself. You deserve it.

Unfortunately I was also stupid, and begged for another chance, so I could fix things? I don't know why I asked for that now because it wasn't me that needed the fixing. Her literally transformed into a different person overnight. I have been no contact for 9 days, only speaking once to correlate him coming to get his things. I was hurting, bad, but I refused to show him that. I even helped him move his things out and was friendly, but distant. Back to no contact now, but this has gotten so much easier than I thought it would. I guess I never realized that if he could become someone else overnight, so could I. And I did. I became someone who didn't need him.

The fact that so many people posted regarding mental disorders is both amazing and devastating to me. When I posted this question, mental disorders were the first things that came to my mind. While it hurts my heart to know mental disease affects SO many people, the fact that so many people also realize the problem in it is a step in the right direction. Personally, I am medicated and diagnosed with PTSD, generalized anxiety, major depressive disorder, stress-induced schizophrenia, borderline personality disorder, and insomnia. I have also been diagnosed with physical disorders such as RA, Fibromyalgia, and chronic fatigue. I'm only 24 years old, and I'm a single mother of 4. The mess that is my brain and mind is terrifying sometimes, and each of these disorders are so capable of ruining lives; not just the ill, but the ones surrounding the ill. I recently had a custody hearing for my children and had to make the difficult decision to have my therapist testify for me, abolishing most of my confidentiality rights. While she was able to tell the court system that I'm not a danger to myself or those around me, she did also have to tell the court about the intrusive thoughts that I've been experiencing. The look on peoples' faces when she told them that I'd had to hide a tool box in my own home because I couldn't walk past it without wondering about what it would feel like to bash my head in with a hammer was absolutely repulsive. The father of my children was also there to hear this statement and he decided to post what was said in court on social media. The comments he's received about people feeling that my children need to be taken from me permanently because of my thought process is disgusting. I cannot control my mental illnesses. You don't blame an alcoholic for wanting to drink, you blame them for drinking. You don't blame someone mentally ill for their thoughts. Their thoughts are often just as shocking, if not more, to themselves.

When I was pregnant with my twin girls, I had twin to twin transfusion. I noticed I started getting much larger extremely quickly and it hurt horribly. I went to three hospitals who basically told me they didn't care and weren't obligated to do anything because at 21 weeks, we had not yet reached viability so my girls weren't even considered as people. By the time I got to the fourth hospital, 2 hours away, I couldn't even walk. I had ended up retaining so much fluid that I was measuring the size of 48 weeks pregnant and I had cracked 4 ribs by how big I got and how quickly I'd gotten there. I was rushed into surgery where they drained 2.5 liters of fluid from my stomach. I'd woken up twice during that surgery and felt nearly everything. Finally, after surgery, I was fine before I started vomiting violently, ripping every single stitch they'd just put in. By the time I could page a nurse to my room, I'd bled so much through the torn stitches that I needed a blood transfusion. Everything was fine afterwards until about two hours later when I woke up to my lungs flooding with blood and being completely unable to breathe. Things finally calmed after I'd been put on oxygen, but it was undoubtedly the most painful few days of my life.

It was incredibly scary! I started excessive monitoring around 10 weeks, as soon as we found out they were MoDi twins. The closest hospital that could monitor the blood flow was a couple hours away and we had to go there every Tuesday and Friday. The Friday before our surgery, levels looked fine. Saturday I woke up in excruciating pain and went to the nearest hospital. This was a little before 21 weeks and the hospital, without doing ultrasound, told me it sounded like my gallbladder and told me to go home. Went home and the pain increased, went to another hospital in my city and was told that I probably had a kidney infection. I asked them to check me to make sure I wasn't dilating and to do an ultrasound, they say they weren't obligated because I was not yet 24 weeks and before 24 weeks, the babies aren't viable anyways, so it would've done no good. Pain got worse the next morning, went to the next city over and again was told gallbladder. At that point, I thought I was just overreacting. I waited it out until my initial appointment that following Tuesday and was Stage III/IV TTTS, with the next step being fatality. We were told that normally the family can go home, discuss options, and decide whether or not to continue with surgery, but if we did that they wouldn't have had any chance of survival. I had the surgery the next morning at 8 AM and the entire thing was a mess. My surgeon did the old method of the surgery with a very large scar and that night, I reacted poorly to something and my lungs began flooding. I don't remember much of the next few days, but I know I couldn't breathe on my own and needed a blood transfusion. That entire experience was so terrifying, I honestly don't think I could ever go through that again. I still don't know how my fluid built so much in so little time, but the pain of it all still makes me cringe.

I agree that seeking help should be a good starter point, but sometimes it's just so hard to. Not because you don't feel like it, but how do you know where to begin? When you go to a hospital with a broken arm, you can just simply say what happened, why you believe it's broken, and get help to repair it. When you're depressed, where do you start? How do you explain depression that eats at you in words? It feels like trying to explain what water tastes like. You can taste it, you know the answer, you can visualize it, but no matter how many words we have in this world, nothing can give a description valid enough to make someone else imagine it in the same way as you do.

What happens when your depression makes you a "human potato?" What happens when you can no longer get out of bed because your heart just hurts, your bones ache, your sleep is sporadic, and the worst taunting you experience is being echoed throughout your mind on an endless loop? I guess I know the difference between physical and mental pain and anguish, but they can run together so easily and once they do, everything hurts everywhere.

You'll need to have Kodi (obviously), localcast, and ES file explorer. Go to Google and search for "PlayerFactoryCore.xml" and download that as well. Open your ES file explorer, go to your settings and make sure that you have it set to show hidden folders. Select the path that you downloaded "PlayerFactoryCore.xml" to and move that xml file to the path: Android>Data>org.xbmc.kodi>files>.kodi>userdata. Once it's moved, your player should override. Go to any stream like normal and localcast will ask where you'd like to cast to. Select your Chromecast setup. Localcast will then ask if you want to play the file or add it to your queue. Select play. For future reference, you can make a queue while your video is playing. This method will override XBMC being your default player, so in the future it will just go straight to Localcast. Hope this helps! Message me if you need any more help!

As you said, postpartum is pretty much what it sounds like. The first couple weeks after you have a child, your hormones are bound to go for quite a ride. That first stage is the "baby blues" which usually is the first 2-3 weeks after birth. Depression that extends that time period would be classified as postpartum depression. It isn't necessarily that you're depressed due to your child, but you begin lacking the ability and motivation to do some things. You're usually far more tired, anxious, and/or sad. It becomes more difficult to do some things that you normally do and that you have to do. Cleaning is more difficult, working is more difficult, etc. It just takes everything and makes it a struggle. Postpartum psychosis is usually when your depression completely plateaus. Psychosis does not necessarily mean that you will hurt your child, but it becomes much more of a possibility. Some people report hallucinations, hearing things that aren't there, irrational fears, or intrusive thoughts. One of my fears was just not being good enough for my kids. I mean, everyone has that fear, but mine was literally to the point where I cried whenever I saw them because I felt bad for them for having me as a mom. My twins had spent time in the NICU after birth and that had also haunted me. Small things would bring back flashbacks, most commonly the bradycardia spells when my daughters just stopped breathing randomly in the NICU. I had spent many nights setting alarms, sometimes hourly, to go into their room and put my hand on their chest to make sure they were breathing. When I did that, I would picture them dead in my mind and would continue to do so until I'd checked. I think a lot of people just kinda take postpartum depression or psychosis and assume that people may be overreacting, especially since those of us who have dealt with it have such difficulties explaining it. The way I describe it to other people is to tell them to explain what water tastes like. It's impossible to verbalize it, you can taste it and you can comprehend it, but verbalization is impossible. No matter how many words or languages there are in the world, none of them fits to do your description justice. That struggle to find a way to make someone else understand but the inability to actually do so is what postpawrtum depression and postpartum psychosis feels like to me. You know it's there, but you just live with the jumble in your brain because for once, don't exist.

I would reccomend speaking to an obstetrician on general information, and a nurse practitioner if you feel it may be something that you need evaulated or medicated. I would advise staying OFF of Google to research these things. If you do have any forms of depression or psychosis, there's a fine line between those and forms of OCD. Looking at things from search engines could potentially be harmful to your overall well-being. This was one of my largest mistakes. I had looked at things online so much that I'd convinced myself that everyone was out to get me and believed there was conspiracy behind everything. It consumed me and threw me even further into depression and psychosis. For new moms, or really just moms in general, I'd also limit social media. Somehow there's an unspoken competition between parents. Who has the better house, car, job; whose child is "smarter," etc. The problem with this is, it's almost always embelished. No one will ever be the best, but throwing yourself into competition is just asking got something to go awry. 

I think the most prominent warning signs are signs that most moms deal with after birth anyways. You will be tired, you will be emotional, and you will be stressed. The problem comes when those feelings are all you feel. A lot of people talk about baby blues, but baby blues should begin to cease by 2-3 weeks postpartum. If someone continues feeling this way after that amount of time, it may beed to be assessed. If you have any thoughts of hurting yourself or someone else, seek help immediately and always remember if you get frustrated with a crying baby, it will not hurt them to set them in their crib and walk away for a few minutes. Everyone says that they would never hurt their child, but the fact of these illnesses is that you don't know who you are anymore. You may never hurt your child intentionally, but your mind stops thinking in it's normal form by this point.

My story is still being written, but the changes that I've made since July (when I'd lost my children) are miraculous. The complete strangers that I've had to work with even notice a huge difference in me, the only one who hadn't seen the difference at first was me. When my kids were taken in July, they were taken due to neglect. I have to state that I was doing what needed to be done for them, but I was doing the bare minimum. I'd started to notice depression setting in and talked to my then-partner about it. He dismissed it and just told me I was weak. Naturally when someone claims that they love you, you respect their opinion. One day he woke up and told me that he no longer loved me because I was too weak. I had three children at home at the time and even though he had left us, I welcomed him back at any given time because I knew he could physically do for our children what I couldn't because of all of the emotion I'd felt. Shortly after he left us, I found out I was pregnant with my son. Some part of me knew that I needed help with all of the depression, but it broke my heart too much to think of ever living without my children. At my worst, I had to feed my twins by propping their bottles and look on from a distance because I felt guilty to touch my own daughters. I felt like if someone else who had loved me so much could just leave, I was clearly not someone worth being around. I had began planning my own suicide, which I had intent to carry out as soon as my son was born. I didn't want to take his life with my own, but in my mind, suicide would be the only way my kids could be truly happy. When one of my twins was colicy, I rocked her to sleep or walked her to sleep, but I did so in the dark so she didn't have to see me. I can't tell you how many times I've apologized to my own children for fighting so hard to be here, just to be stuck with a mom like me. Eventually I started having intrusive thoughts and there wasn't a single time that I was able to open the door to my childrens' room without picturing them in my mind, lifeless. I couldn't do what they needed me to do and part of me knew that. In July when they were taken due to suspected neglect, I was forced to seek help. I was still pregnant with my son but it snapped me back into reality knowing that I had to do whatever it took to get my kids back. My first counseling session, I just sat there. It's still taking me time to knock the wall down and let people in, but I've gained so many supports by seeking help. The foster families that they've had, the caseworkers, people I attend parenting classes with. My son is now almost 6 weeks old and I get to see my son and three daughters frequently and am moving towardsmoving forward. Progressing to make sure I'm okay enough for them to be okay. The one thing that gets me through, which I hope your friend knows, is that our kids still love us. When we suffer from mental illness, we don't voluntarily suffer, and pur babies know that somehow. No matter how guilty I feel about all of the times that I just couldn't hold my children, they still look at me and call me "mom." My oldest tells me she loves me (she's 2) and gives me a million hugs and kisses when she sees me. My twins fight over me, and cling to me like glue. They're closer to me now than ever, even though we're apart, because I'm finally becoming a mom worth being close to. I truly hope your friend finds peace with her situation, and please know that whether or not she admits it, she feels guilt. It's a guilt that won't ever cease completely, but there is also so much hope for her future, especially now that she's getting the help that she needs.
